claim: Microstimulating mouse superior colliculus (SC) elicits directed head and eye movements resembling SC-dependent sensory-guided gaze shifts in other species.
source: However, microstimulating mouse superior colliculus (SC) elicits directed head and eye movements resembling SC-dependent sensory-guided gaze shifts in other species, suggesting that mouse gaze shifts may be more flexible than has been recognized.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (implied by the statement) and is consistent with the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Tactile stimuli evoke directionally biased saccades coincident with attempted head rotations in head-fixed mice.
source: We found tactile stimuli evoke directionally biased saccades coincident with attempted head rotations.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figures 2-4.

claim: Differences in saccade endpoints across stimuli are associated with distinct stimulus-dependent relationships between initial eye position and saccade direction and amplitude.
source: Differences in saccade endpoints across stimuli are associated with distinct stimulus-dependent relationships between initial eye position and saccade direction and amplitude.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Superior colliculus drives touch-evoked gaze shifts in head-fixed mice.
source: Optogenetic perturbations revealed SC drives these gaze shifts.
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic manipulation experiments presented in Figure 6.

claim: SC optogenetic stimulation elicits contraversive eye and attempted head movements.
source: Consonant with previous studies, SC optogenetic stimulation elicited contraversive eye and attempted head movements (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and D and is consistent with previous studies.

claim: Optogenetically evoked saccades and attempted head movements are roughly coincident.
source: Strikingly, optogenetically evoked saccades and attempted head movements were roughly coincident, similar to what has been described for SC-dependent sensory-guided gaze shifts in other species and unlike the temporal relationship previously documented for mouse spontaneous and visually evoked gaze shifts (Figure 1C and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and E and comparison with previous literature.

claim: The probability of horizontal eye movements increased significantly above baseline in the 100ms period following delivery of multisensory airpuffs.
source: The probability of horizontal eye movements increased sharply and significantly above the low baseline level (1.3% ± 0.2%, mean ± s.d.) in the 100ms period following delivery of multisensory airpuffs (ear airpuff: 29.0% ± 7.5%, p < 0.001 paired Student's t-test; whisker airpuff: 12.5% ± 2.3%, p < 0.001), auditory airpuffs (3.5% ± 1.2%, p < 0.05), and tactile stimuli (4.5% ± 0.5%, p < 0.001) and remained slightly elevated for at least 500 ms (Figure 2B–F and G–K; Figure 2—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The probability of saccade generation was not changed by visual stimuli.
source: In contrast, the probability of saccade generation was not changed by visual stimuli (Figure 2F and K; 1.3% ± 0.2%, p = 0.61).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2F and K.

claim: Stimulus-evoked eye movements are saccades because they reached velocities of several hundred degrees per second.
source: We consider these stimulus-evoked eye movements to be saccades because they reached velocities of several hundred degrees per second (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), displayed a main sequence, that is, peak velocity scaled linearly with amplitude (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and were bilaterally conjugate (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Bahill et al., 1975).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and citation to Bahill et al., 1975.

claim: Auditory, tactile, and audiotactile stimuli evoked attempted head movements but visual stimuli did not.
source: Mirroring results for saccades, auditory, tactile, and audiotactile stimuli evoked attempted head movements but visual stimuli did not (Figure 2L–P; auditory: 53.2% ± 21.9%, p = 0.045; tactile: 67.1% ± 10%, p < 0.01; ear airpuff: 86.6% ± 8.7%, p < 10–5; whisker airpuff: 79.2% ± 9.5%, p < 0.001; visual: 26.9% ± 2.0%, p = 0.0505, paired Student's t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2L-P.

claim: Left ear airpuffs evoked saccades with endpoints far left of center, whereas right ear airpuffs evoked saccades with endpoints far right of center.
source: We found that left ear airpuffs evoked saccades with endpoints far left of center (with center defined as the mean eye position), whereas right ear airpuffs evoked saccades with endpoints far right of center (left: –5.4 ± 4.5°, right: 5.4 ± 3.4°, mean ± s.d., p < 10–10 Welch's t-test, n = 2155 trials).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Left ear airpuffs elicited nearly exclusively leftward saccades (94.2% ± 3.1%), whereas right ear airpuffs elicited nearly exclusively rightward saccades (96.0% ± 2.1%).
source: We found that left ear airpuffs elicited nearly exclusively leftward saccades (94.2% ± 3.1%, mean ± s.d., n = 5 mice), whereas right ear airpuffs elicited nearly exclusively rightward saccades (96.0% ± 2.1%)—often from the same eye positions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data analysis.

claim: Airpuffs applied to the whiskers evoked saccades with endpoints central to those evoked by ear airpuff stimulation.
source: Indeed, airpuffs applied to the whiskers evoked saccades with endpoints central to those evoked by ear airpuff stimulation, such that the ordering of saccade endpoints mirrored that of stimulus locations (Mean endpoints: left ear, –5.4 ± 4.5°; left whiskers, –0.4 ± 3.8°; right whiskers, 0.8 ± 3.9°; right ear, 5.4 ± 3.4°; mean ± s.d., p < 0.05 for all pairwise comparisons, paired two-tailed Student's t-test) (Figure 3A and B; Figure 3—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Tactile stimuli delivered to the left and right ears evoked saccades whose endpoints were significantly different.
source: Similar to the multisensory airpuff stimuli, tactile stimuli delivered to the left and right ears evoked saccades whose endpoints were significantly different (–3.9 ± 5.3° [left] vs. 1.5 ± 5.0° [right]; mean ± s.d., p < 10–10, Welch's t-test, n = 452 trials) and whose directions were largely opposite from nearly all eye positions (Figure 3C and G, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) (left stimuli evoked 77.5% ± 23.7% leftward saccades, right stimuli evoked 78.3% ± 11.6% rightward saccades, n = 5 mice).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3C and G.

claim: The endpoint locations did not differ significantly for saccades elicited by left and right auditory stimuli and were located centrally.
source: Strikingly, the endpoint locations did not differ significantly for saccades elicited by left and right auditory stimuli and were located centrally (0.1 ± 5.1° (left) vs. –0.1 ± 5.1° (right); mean ± s.d., p = 0.72, Welch's t-test, n = 298 trials).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Saccades evoked by both right and left auditory stimuli traveled in the same, centripetal direction from all initial eye positions.
source: The central endpoints of sound-evoked saccades arose because, in contrast to touch-evoked saccades, saccades evoked by both right and left stimuli traveled in the same, centripetal direction from all initial eye positions: rightward from eye positions to the left of center, and leftward from eye positions to the right of center (fraction centripetal: left airpuff for initial eye positions left of center, 0.89 ± 0.08; left airpuff for initial eye positions right of center, 0.90 ± 0.09; right airpuff for initial eye positions left of center, 0.87 ± 0.07; right airpuff with initial eye positions right of center, 0.76 ± 0.12).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data analysis.

claim: The mean sound-evoked saccade endpoint was not significantly different from the mean overall eye position, suggesting that sound-evoked saccades function to center the eye.
source: We compared the mean sound-evoked saccade endpoint to the mean overall eye position and found no significant difference, suggesting that sound-evoked saccades function to center the eye (p = 0.93, one-sample Student's t-test) (Land and Nilsson, 2012; Meyer et al., 2018; Meyer et al., 2020; Michaiel et al., 2020; Paré and Munoz, 2001; Tatler, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and citations to previous literature.

claim: The amplitude distributions for attempted head movements to left and right ear airpuff stimuli were well separated.
source: The amplitude distributions for attempted head movements to left and right ear airpuff stimuli were well separated (left: –1.56 ± 1.25 Z, right: 1.29 ± 1.16 Z, mean ± s.d., p < 10–10 Welch's t-test, n = 2155 trials), mirroring the separation of the endpoints of saccades elicited by left and right stimuli (Figure 3I).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Whisker and tactile stimuli elicited attempted head movements whose amplitude distributions were separated but less so than those of ear airpuffs.
source: Similarly, whisker and tactile stimuli elicited attempted head movements whose amplitude distributions were separated (left whiskers: –0.22 ± 1.58 Z, right whiskers: 0.20 ± 1.42 Z, p < 10–4, n = 1046; left tactile: –1.45 ± 1.84 Z, right tactile: 0.55 ± 1.75 Z, p < 10–10, n = 319; mean ± s.d., Welch's t-test) but less so than those of ear airpuffs (Figure 3J and K).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3J and K.

claim: Left and right auditory airpuffs elicited attempted head movements whose distributions overlapped.
source: Left and right auditory airpuffs elicited attempted head movements whose distributions overlapped (left: –0.25 ± 2.04 Z, right: 0.07 ± 1.94 Z, mean ± s.d., p = 0.16, Welch's t-test, n = 298 trials), similar to what was observed for saccades (Figure 3L).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3L.

claim: Most spontaneous saccades were preceded by attempted head rotations in the same direction as the ensuing saccade.
source: Consistent with these observations, we found that most spontaneous saccades were preceded by attempted head rotations in the same direction as the ensuing saccade (Figure 4B, D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B, D and E.

claim: Attempted head rotations during spontaneous saccades appeared biphasic, with a slow phase starting 100–200 ms before saccade onset followed by a fast phase beginning roughly simultaneously with saccade onset.
source: Interestingly, attempted head rotations during spontaneous saccades appeared biphasic, with a slow phase starting 100–200 ms before saccade onset followed by a fast phase beginning roughly simultaneously with saccade onset (Figure 4B, D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B, D and E.

claim: Ear airpuff-evoked saccades were typically not preceded by slow attempted head rotations but were accompanied by roughly coincident fast attempted head rotations.
source: Consistent with our prediction, ear airpuff-evoked saccades were typically not preceded by slow attempted head rotations but were accompanied by roughly coincident fast attempted head rotations (Figure 4B, D and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B, D and F.

claim: For spontaneous gaze shifts, attempted head movement onset fell along a continuum starting well before saccade onset, with attempted head displacement roughly 60% predictive of the direction of the ensuing saccade starting as early as 200 ms before saccade onset and approximately 80% predictive by 100 ms before saccade onset.
source: For spontaneous gaze shifts, attempted head movement onset fell along a continuum starting well before saccade onset, with attempted head displacement roughly 60% predictive of the direction of the ensuing saccade starting as early as 200 ms before saccade onset and approximately 80% predictive by 100 ms before saccade onset (Figure 4E and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and G.

claim: For stimulus-evoked gaze shifts, the vast majority of attempted head movements began roughly coincidently with saccade onset, and attempted head displacement was not predictive of head position prior to saccade onset.
source: In contrast, for stimulus-evoked gaze shifts, the vast majority of attempted head movements began roughly coincidently with saccade onset, and attempted head displacement was not predictive of head position prior to saccade onset (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F and G.

claim: Stimulus-evoked saccades of a given amplitude were coupled to an average of 24% smaller attempted head movements than were spontaneous saccades.
source: Interestingly, stimulus-evoked saccades of a given amplitude were coupled to an average of 24% smaller attempted head movements than were spontaneous saccades (linear regression slopes 0.162 vs 0.214, p < 10–5, permutation test) (Figure 4H).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The difference in head-eye coupling between spontaneous and evoked saccades was due to the slow pre-saccadic attempted head movements observed during spontaneous gaze shifts, as the fast phase of both spontaneous and evoked gaze shifts was nearly identical.
source: This difference was due to the slow pre-saccadic attempted head movements observed during spontaneous gaze shifts, as the fast phase of both spontaneous and evoked gaze shifts was nearly identical (Figure 4L).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4L.

claim: Endpoints for attempted head movement-matched whisker and ear airpuff trials remained well-separated, indicating that the more directionally biased endpoints of ear airpuff-evoked saccades are not simply due to larger or more directionally biased attempted head movements.
source: Strikingly, however, endpoints for attempted head movement-matched whisker and ear airpuff trials remained well-separated, indicating that the more directionally biased endpoints of ear airpuff-evoked saccades are not simply due to larger or more directionally biased attempted head movements (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: For all stimuli there was an inverse relationship between initial eye position and saccade amplitude but the slopes and intercepts of the lines of best fit describing these relationships differed depending on stimulus modality and location.
source: Indeed, for all stimuli there was an inverse relationship between initial eye position and saccade amplitude but the slopes and intercepts of the lines of best fit describing these relationships differed depending on stimulus modality and location (Figure 5A–D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A-D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Initial eye position strongly influenced saccade probability, and the relationship between initial eye position and saccade probability differed across stimuli, with the lowest probability coinciding with the mean endpoint of saccades evoked by that stimulus.
source: Indeed, initial eye position strongly influenced saccade probability, and the relationship between initial eye position and saccade probability differed across stimuli, with the lowest probability coinciding with the mean endpoint of saccades evoked by that stimulus (Figure 5I–L, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5I-L and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Saccade probability did not differ between trials with high (dilated pupils) or low (constricted pupils) arousal.
source: In contrast, saccade probability did not differ between trials with high (dilated pupils) or low (constricted pupils) arousal (Figure 5—figure supplement 3; Reimer et al., 2014) and declined only slightly over successive sessions or within sessions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3 and citation to Reimer et al., 2014.

claim: Attempted head movement direction and amplitude were dependent on initial eye position for whisker airpuff-evoked gaze shifts.
source: Strikingly, attempted head movement direction and amplitude were dependent on initial eye position (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: For auditory airpuff-evoked gaze shifts, both attempted head movement direction and amplitude were dependent on initial eye position.
source: As for whisker airpuffs, both attempted head movement direction and amplitude were dependent on initial eye position (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: For ear tactile stimuli, attempted head movement direction and amplitude depended on eye position, but the slope of this relationship was shallower.
source: Indeed, as for both whisker and auditory airpuffs, attempted head movement direction and amplitude depended on eye position, but the slope of this relationship was shallower (Figure 5G, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Eye position strongly influenced the probability of attempted head movements evoked by all stimuli, including ear airpuffs.
source: However, eye position strongly influenced the probability of attempted head movements evoked by all stimuli, including ear airpuffs (Figure 5M–P, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5M-P and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: For all stimuli, initial eye position was a much stronger predictor of saccade direction and amplitude than was initial position of the head.
source: For all stimuli, initial eye position was a much stronger predictor of saccade direction and amplitude than was initial position of the head (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: Optically reducing right SC activity shifted airpuff-evoked saccade endpoints to the right (i.e. ipsilaterally) for both left and right ear airpuffs.
source: Consistent with data in foveate species (Hikosaka and Wurtz, 1985; Robinson, 1972; Schiller and Stryker, 1972), optically reducing right SC activity shifted airpuff-evoked saccade endpoints to the right (i.e. ipsilaterally) for both left (–3.7 ± 4.3° [control] vs. –2.3 ± 4.7° [LED on], p < 0.001, Welch's t-test) and right ear airpuffs (4.5 ± 4.1° [control] vs. 5.4 ± 4.7° [LED on], p = 0.011, Welch's t-test) (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A-C and citations to previous literature (Hikosaka and Wurtz, 1985; Robinson, 1972; Schiller and Stryker, 1972).

claim: Weak SC stimulation caused the reciprocal effect of right SC inhibition, biasing endpoints leftwards (i.e. contraversively) for both left and right airpuffs.
source: This manipulation caused the reciprocal effect of right SC inhibition, biasing endpoints leftwards (i.e. contraversively) for both left (–5.8 ± 4.6° [control] vs. –8.0 ± 6.1° [LED on], p = 0.0016, Welch's t-test) and right (5.6 ± 3.5° [control] vs. 1.9 ± 6.1° [LED on], p < 10–5, Welch's t-test) airpuffs (Figure 6E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E-G.

claim: SC manipulations had no effect on the relationship between saccade and head movement amplitudes, suggesting that SC manipulations do not change head-eye coupling during gaze shifts.
source: Interestingly, SC manipulations had no effect on the relationship between saccade and head movement amplitudes, suggesting that SC manipulations do not change head-eye coupling during gaze shifts (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The prevailing view holds that mouse gaze shifts are led by head rotations followed by brainstem-mediated eye movements, including saccades to reset the eyes.
source: In the prevailing view, mouse gaze shifts entail head rotations followed by brainstem-mediated eye movements, including saccades to reset the eyes.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific consensus and previous literature.

claim: Recentering saccades are attributed to head movement-related vestibular cues.
source: These 'recentering' saccades are attributed to head movement-related vestibular cues.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific consensus and previous literature.

claim: Recent studies tracking head and eye movements in freely moving mice found that spontaneous and visually evoked mouse gaze shifts matched the description of head-led gaze shifts with recentering saccades.
source: Indeed, recent studies tracking head and eye movements in freely moving mice found that spontaneous and visually evoked mouse gaze shifts matched this description (Meyer et al., 2018; Meyer et al., 2020; Michaiel et al., 2020; Payne and Raymond, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Meyer et al., 2018; Meyer et al., 2020; Michaiel et al., 2020; Payne and Raymond, 2017).

claim: During a gaze shift in freely moving mice, slow eye movements stabilize the retinal image by countering the rotation of the head and are punctuated by fast saccadic eye movements to recenter the eyes in the orbits as they approach the end of their range of motion.
source: Specifically, during a gaze shift, slow eye movements stabilize the retinal image by countering the rotation of the head and are punctuated by fast saccadic eye movements to recenter the eyes in the orbits as they approach the end of their range of motion.
evidence: This claim is based on previous studies in freely moving mice.

claim: Recentering saccades are centripetal, occur in the direction of the head movement, and are thought to be driven by vestibular or optokinetic signals acting on circuits in brainstem.
source: These recentering saccades—also known as 'compensatory' saccades or the quick phase of nystagmus—are centripetal, occur in the direction of the head movement, and are thought to be driven by vestibular or optokinetic signals acting on circuits in brainstem (Curthoys, 2002; Hepp et al., 1993; Kitama et al., 1995; Meyer et al., 2020; Michaiel et al., 2020; Payne and Raymond, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Curthoys, 2002; Hepp et al., 1993; Kitama et al., 1995; Meyer et al., 2020; Michaiel et al., 2020; Payne and Raymond, 2017).

claim: Primates and other foveate species are capable of an additional form of gaze shift led by directed saccades, with or without directed head movements, to redirect their gaze toward salient stimuli.
source: In contrast, primates and other foveate species are capable of an additional form of gaze shift led by directed saccades, with or without directed head movements, to redirect their gaze toward salient stimuli (Bizzi et al., 1972; Freedman, 2008; Lee, 1999; Zangemeister and Stark, 1982).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Bizzi et al., 1972; Freedman, 2008; Lee, 1999; Zangemeister and Stark, 1982).

claim: Directed saccades differ from recentering saccades in that they have endpoints specified by the location of the stimulus, typically occur simultaneously with head movements during gaze shifts, and are driven by midbrain circuits, particularly the superior colliculus (SC).
source: Directed saccades differ from recentering saccades in that they have endpoints specified by the location of the stimulus (and therefore are often centrifugally directed), typically occur simultaneously with head movements during gaze shifts, and are driven by midbrain circuits, particularly the superior colliculus (SC).
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about directed saccades.

claim: To date, there is no behavioral evidence that mice or any afoveate species generate directed saccades or gaze shifts not initiated by head movements.
source: To date, there is no behavioral evidence that mice or any afoveate species generate directed saccades or gaze shifts not initiated by head movements.
evidence: This claim is based on a review of existing literature.

claim: Head-fixed mice generate saccades, albeit less frequently than freely moving mice.
source: First, mouse saccades are not only a product of vestibular or optokinetic cues, because head-fixed mice, in which these signals do not occur, generate saccades, albeit less frequently.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that head-fixed mice make saccades without vestibular or optokinetic cues.

claim: Microstimulation of the mouse superior colliculus (SC) showed that it contains a topographic map of saccade and head movement direction and amplitude.
source: Specifically, microstimulation of the mouse superior colliculus (SC) showed that it contains a topographic map of saccade and head movement direction and amplitude (Masullo et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2015) roughly aligned with maps of visual, auditory, and somatosensory space (Dräger and Hubel, 1975).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Masullo et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2015; Dräger and Hubel, 1975).

claim: SC sensory and motor maps in mice resemble those believed to underlie primates' and cats' ability to make gaze shifts led by directed saccades toward stimuli of visual, auditory, and somatosensory modalities.
source: These SC sensory and motor maps resemble those believed to underlie primates' and cats' ability to make gaze shifts led by directed saccades toward stimuli of these modalities (Sparks, 1986; Sparks, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Sparks, 1986; Sparks, 2002).

claim: Saccade-like eye movements in the absence of head movements have occasionally been observed in freely moving mice, albeit infrequently and usually in close proximity to head movements.
source: Third, saccade-like eye movements in the absence of head movements have occasionally been observed in freely moving mice, albeit infrequently and usually in close proximity to head movements (Meyer et al., 2018; Meyer et al., 2020; Michaiel et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Meyer et al., 2018; Meyer et al., 2020; Michaiel et al., 2020).

claim: There is evidence in humans, non-human primates, and cats that gaze shifts in response to different sensory modalities can involve distinct head-eye coupling strategies.
source: Second, previous analyses in mice were mostly confined to spontaneous or visually guided gaze shifts, and there is evidence in humans, non-human primates, and cats that gaze shifts in response to different sensory modalities can involve distinct head-eye coupling strategies (Goldring et al., 1996; Populin, 2006; Populin and Rajala, 2011; Populin et al., 2004; Ruhland et al., 2013; Tollin et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Goldring et al., 1996; Populin, 2006; Populin and Rajala, 2011; Populin et al., 2004; Ruhland et al., 2013; Tollin et al., 2005).

claim: Saccade size for temporal-to-nasal movements was slightly larger than for nasal-to-temporal movements.
source: As in previous studies, saccade size for temporal-to-nasal movements was slightly larger than for nasal-to-temporal movements (Meyer et al., 2018), but this asymmetry was eliminated by averaging the positions of both pupils (before averaging: temporal saccade amplitude = 10.9 ± 0.8° (mean ± s.d.), nasal saccade amplitude = 8.4 ± 1.1°, p = 0.0009; after averaging, leftward amplitude = 10.2 ± 1.0°, rightward amplitude = 9.3 ± 0.4°, p = 0.0986).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citation to Meyer et al., 2018.

claim: The baseline frequency of attempted head movements was much higher than that of eye movements (27.8% ± 4.8%, mean ± s.d.).
source: We next examined attempted head movements. The baseline frequency of attempted head movements was much higher than that of eye movements (27.8% ± 4.8%, mean ± s.d.).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The airpuffs were <65 dB.
source: These responses are unlikely to be due to an auditory startle response, which is elicited by stimuli louder than 80 dB, because the airpuffs were <65 dB (Gómez-Nieto et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurement and citation to Gómez-Nieto et al., 2020.

claim: Both the auditory and tactile components of the airpuff stimuli are sufficient to evoke saccades but only tactile stimulation evokes directionally biased saccades whose endpoints are specified by the site of stimulation.
source: Thus, both the auditory and tactile components of the airpuff stimuli are sufficient to evoke saccades but only tactile stimulation evokes directionally biased saccades whose endpoints are specified by the site of stimulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing auditory and tactile stimuli.

claim: This biphasic response closely resembles the eye-head coupling pattern reported in freely moving mice.
source: This biphasic response closely resembles the eye-head coupling pattern reported in freely moving mice (Meyer et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Meyer et al., 2020.

claim: The gain of head-eye coupling did appear significantly lower for evoked but not spontaneous gaze shifts by the fifth session.
source: Interestingly, the gain of head-eye coupling did appear significantly lower for evoked but not spontaneous gaze shifts by the fifth session, but at every time point analyzed, evoked gaze shifts involved smaller head movements than did spontaneous gaze shifts (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Differences between spontaneous and evoked gaze shifts do not reflect learning.
source: These data indicate that mice may subtly and slowly change their strategies with experience but differences between spontaneous and evoked gaze shifts do not reflect learning.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing persistent differences across sessions.

claim: Starting eye position and stimulus location jointly shape attempted head and eye movement probability, direction, and amplitude.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that starting eye position and stimulus location jointly shape attempted head and eye movement probability, direction, and amplitude.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: In other species, stimulus-evoked gaze shifts involving directed head and eye movements are driven by SC.
source: As discussed previously, in other species, stimulus-evoked gaze shifts involving directed head and eye movements are driven by SC (Freedman, 2008; Freedman et al., 1996; Guitton, 1992; Guitton et al., 1980; Paré et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Freedman, 2008; Freedman et al., 1996; Guitton, 1992; Guitton et al., 1980; Paré et al., 1994).

claim: It is widely believed that the recentering saccades observed in mice are driven by brainstem circuitry in response to head rotation.
source: In contrast, it is widely believed that the recentering saccades observed in mice are driven by brainstem circuitry in response to head rotation (Curthoys, 2002; Hepp et al., 1993; Kitama et al., 1995; Meyer et al., 2020; Michaiel et al., 2020; Payne and Raymond, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Curthoys, 2002; Hepp et al., 1993; Kitama et al., 1995; Meyer et al., 2020; Michaiel et al., 2020; Payne and Raymond, 2017).

claim: Reducing right SC activity is consistent with data in foveate species.
source: Consistent with data in foveate species (Hikosaka and Wurtz, 1985; Robinson, 1972; Schiller and Stryker, 1972), optically reducing right SC activity shifted airpuff-evoked saccade endpoints to the right (i.e. ipsilaterally) for both left (–3.7 ± 4.3° [control] vs. –2.3 ± 4.7° [LED on], p < 0.001, Welch's t-test) and right ear airpuffs (4.5 ± 4.1° [control] vs. 5.4 ± 4.7° [LED on], p = 0.011, Welch's t-test) (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to previous literature (Hikosaka and Wurtz, 1985; Robinson, 1972; Schiller and Stryker, 1972).

claim: These bidirectional manipulations indicate that SC serves a conserved necessary and sufficient role in generating ear airpuff-evoked gaze shifts.
source: Taken together, these bidirectional manipulations indicate that SC serves a conserved necessary and sufficient role in generating ear airpuff-evoked gaze shifts.
evidence: This claim is supported by the optogenetic manipulation experiments.

claim: SC manipulations suggest that SC specifies the overall gaze shift amplitude rather than the individual eye or head movement components, consistent with observations in other species.
source: This observation suggests that SC specifies the overall gaze shift amplitude rather than the individual eye or head movement components, consistent with observations in other species (Freedman et al., 1996; Paré et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to previous literature (Freedman et al., 1996; Paré et al., 1994).

claim: The discovery that sensory-guided directionally biased saccades are present in head-fixed mice raises the question of what fovea-independent functions these movements ordinarily serve.
source: Our discovery that sensory-guided directionally biased saccades are present in head-fixed mice—albeit withless precise targeting of stimulus location than is seen in foveate species—raises the question of what fovea-independent functions these movements ordinarily serve.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental findings.

claim: Saccades that shift gaze in the direction of a stimulus may facilitate keeping salient stimuli within the field of view.
source: Although mice have lateral eyes and a large field of view, saccades that shift gaze in the direction of a stimulus, as seems to occur with both ear and whisker tactile stimuli, may facilitate keeping salient stimuli within the field of view.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about the functional significance of the observed behavior.

claim: Directing non-visual stimuli toward the center of view maximizes the likelihood of detecting the visual component of the stimulus.
source: As natural stimuli are often multimodal, directing non-visual stimuli toward the center of view maximizes the likelihood of detecting the visual component of the stimulus.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about the functional significance of the observed behavior.

claim: Despite mouse retinae lacking discrete, anatomically defined specializations such as foveae or areas centralis, there are subtler nonuniformities in the distribution and density of photoreceptors and retinal ganglion cell subtypes.
source: Alternatively, despite mouse retinae lacking discrete, anatomically defined specializations such as foveae or areas centralis, there are subtler nonuniformities in the distribution and density of photoreceptors and retinal ganglion cell subtypes, and magnification factor, receptive field sizes, and response tuning vary across the visual field in higher visual centers; it may be desirable to center a salient tactile stimulus on a particular retinal region (Ahmadlou and Heimel, 2015; Baden et al., 2013; van Beest et al., 2021; Bleckert et al., 2014; Dräger and Hubel, 1976; Feinberg and Meister, 2015; Li et al., 2020; de Malmazet et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Ahmadlou and Heimel, 2015; Baden et al., 2013; van Beest et al., 2021; Bleckert et al., 2014; Dräger and Hubel, 1976; Feinberg and Meister, 2015; Li et al., 2020; de Malmazet et al., 2018).

claim: Touch-evoked saccades alone may be too small to center the stimulus location on any particular region of the retina, but they may do so in concert with directed head movements.
source: Although touch-evoked saccades alone may be too small to center the stimulus location on any particular region of the retina, they may do so in concert with directed head movements.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about the functional significance of the observed behavior.

claim: The speed of saccades relative to head movements may be especially beneficial because tactile stimuli typically derive from proximal objects and as a result may demand rapid responses.
source: One possibility is the aforementioned speed of saccades relative to head movements may be especially beneficial because tactile stimuli typically derive from proximal objects and as a result may demand rapid responses.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about why tactile stimuli evoke directionally biased saccades.

claim: The high spatial acuity of the tactile system may enable more precise localization.
source: Alternatively, the high spatial acuity of the tactile system may enable more precise localization (Allen and Ison, 2010; Diamond et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is based on speculation and citations to previous literature (Allen and Ison, 2010; Diamond et al., 2008).

claim: Auditory stimuli may alert animals to the presence of a salient stimulus in their environments whose location is less precisely ascertained, and as a result drive gaze shifts whose goal is to reset the eyes to a central position that maximizes their chances of sensing and responding appropriately.
source: Auditory stimuli, in contrast, may alert animals to the presence of a salient stimulus in their environments whose location is less precisely ascertained, and as a result drive gaze shifts whose goal is to reset the eyes to a central position that maximizes their chances of sensing and responding appropriately.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about the functional significance of auditory-evoked gaze shifts.

claim: In freely moving primates and cats, gaze shifts are led by directed saccades but typically followed by head movements during which the eyes counterrotate centripetally in order to maintain gaze in the new direction.
source: For example, as noted previously, whereas head-fixed primates and cats generate gaze shifts using directed saccades and then maintain their eyes in the new orbital position, similar to what we have observed, in freely moving primates and cats, gaze shifts are led by directed saccades but typically followed by head movements during which the eyes counterrotate centripetally in order to maintain gaze in the new direction.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about gaze shifts in primates and cats.

claim: A practical implication of our identification of mouse SC-dependent gaze shifts is that this behavioral paradigm could be applied to the study of several outstanding questions.
source: Furthermore, a practical implication of our identification of mouse SC-dependent gaze shifts is that this behavioral paradigm could be applied to the study of several outstanding questions.
evidence: This claim is based on inference about the potential applications of the findings.

claim: The mouse provides a genetically tractable platform with which to investigate circuitry and ensemble dynamics underlying target selection and saccade generation.
source: First, there are many unresolved problems regarding the circuitry and ensemble dynamics underlying target selection (Basso and May, 2017) and saccade generation (Gandhi and Katnani, 2011), and the mouse provides a genetically tractable platform with which to investigate these and other topics.
evidence: This claim is based on inference and citations to previous literature (Basso and May, 2017; Gandhi and Katnani, 2011).

claim: Gaze shifts are aberrant in a host of conditions, such as Parkinson's and autism spectrum disorder.
source: Second, gaze shifts are aberrant in a host of conditions, such as Parkinson's and autism spectrum disorder (Liversedge et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Liversedge et al., 2011.

claim: This paradigm could be a powerful tool for the study of mouse models of a variety of neuropsychiatric conditions.
source: This paradigm could be a powerful tool for the study of mouse models of a variety of neuropsychiatric conditions.
evidence: This claim is based on inference about the potential applications of the findings.

claim: Neural correlates of remapping from sensory to motor reference frames have been observed in primates and cats, but the underlying circuitry and computations remain obscure.
source: Neural correlates of this process have been observed in primates (Groh and Sparks, 1996; Jay and Sparks, 1984) and cats (Populin et al., 2004), but the underlying circuitry and computations remain obscure.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Groh and Sparks, 1996; Jay and Sparks, 1984; Populin et al., 2004).

claim: Prior studies in species whose retinae lack high-acuity specializations had never observed gaze shifts with properties of directionally biased saccades coincident with head movements.
source: Prior studies in species whose retinae lack high-acuity specializations had never observed gaze shifts with these properties, but our study used a broader range of stimuli than previously tested and a head-fixed preparation that allowed spatially precise delivery.
evidence: This claim is based on a review of existing literature.

claim: Detailed perturbation experiments determined that the circuit mechanisms of sensory-evoked gaze shifts are conserved from mice to primates.
source: Detailed perturbation experiments determined that the circuit mechanisms of sensory-evoked gaze shifts are conserved from mice to primates, suggesting that this behavior may have arisen in a common, afoveate ancestral species long ago.
evidence: This claim is supported by the optogenetic manipulation experiments and is an inference about evolutionary conservation.

claim: This behavior may have arisen in a common, afoveate ancestral species long ago.
source: Detailed perturbation experiments determined that the circuit mechanisms of sensory-evoked gaze shifts are conserved from mice to primates, suggesting that this behavior may have arisen in a common, afoveate ancestral species long ago.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about the evolutionary origins of the behavior.

claim: Analyzing eye movements of other afoveate species thought not to make directed saccades in response to a diverse range of multimodal stimuli may uncover similar flexibility.
source: More broadly, our findings suggest that analyzing eye movements of other afoveate species thought not to make directed saccades—such as rabbits, toads, and goldfish—in response to a diverse range of multimodal stimuli may uncover similar flexibility.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the findings in mice to other afoveate species.

claim: C57BL/6J wild-type mice between 2 and 6 months of age were used.
source: C57BL/6J wild-type (Jackson Laboratory, stock 000664) mice between 2 and 6 months of age were used.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental methods.

claim: Mice were housed in a vivarium with a reversed 12:12 h light:dark cycle and tested during the dark phase.
source: Mice were housed in a vivarium with a reversed 12:12 h light:dark cycle and tested during the dark phase.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental methods.

claim: Saccades were defined as eye movements that exceeded 100°/s, were at least 3° in amplitude, and were not preceded by a saccade in the previous 100 ms.
source: Saccades were defined as eye movements that exceeded 100°/s, were at least 3° in amplitude, and were not preceded by a saccade in the previous 100 ms.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental methods.

claim: Saccades were defined as being evoked by a sensory or optogenetic stimulus if they occurred within a 100 ms response window following stimulus delivery.
source: For all subsequent analyses, saccades were defined as being evoked by a sensory or optogenetic stimulus if they occurred within a 100 ms response window following stimulus delivery, selected due to the sharp increase in saccade probability during this period (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental methods and is supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Spontaneous saccades were defined as any saccades made outside of an experimental stimulus (i.e. no stimulus in the 500 ms periods preceding or following the saccade).
source: Spontaneous saccades were a catch-all category defined as any saccades made outside of an experimental stimulus (i.e. no stimulus in the 500 ms periods preceding or following the saccade).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental methods.
